name: Gooseberry Wine
description: Historical recipe from Miss Leslie's Complete Cookery (1851). Source method; not modernized or kitchen-tested.

ingredients.name: three-quarters of a pound of loaf-sugar per quart of juice
ingredients.originalText: three-quarters of a pound of loaf-sugar per quart of juice

ingredients.name: white brandy for every gallon of the gooseberry wine
ingredients.originalText: 1 pint of white brandy for every gallon of the gooseberry wine

ingredients.name: very small tea-spoonful of salt
ingredients.originalText: a very small tea-spoonful of salt

instructions.text: Top and tail the gooseberries; put them, a few at a time, into a wooden dish, and with a rolling-pin or beetle break and mash every one; transferring them, as they are done, into a large stone jar
Pour the boiling water upon the mashed gooseberries; cover the jar, and let them stand twelve hours
Then strain and measure the juice, and to each quart allow three-quarters of a pound of loaf-sugar
Mix it with the liquid, and let it stand eight or nine hours to dissolve, stirring it several times
Then pour it into a keg of proper size for containing it, and let it ferment at the bung-hole; filling it up as it works out with some of the liquor reserved for that purpose
As soon as it ceases to hiss, stop it close with a cloth wrapped round the bung
A pint of white brandy for every gallon of the gooseberry wine may be added on bunging it up
At the end of four or five months it will probably be fine enough to bottle off
You may refine it by allowing to every gallon of wine the whites of two eggs, beaten to a froth, with a very small tea-spoonful of salt
When the white of egg, &c. is a stiff froth, take out a quart of the wine, and mix them well together
Then pour it into the cask, and in a few days it will be fine and clear
Put two or three raisins in the bottom of each bottle
Keep the bottles in saw-dust, lying on their sides

source.author: Eliza Leslie
source.originalInstructions:
1. Top and tail the gooseberries; put them, a few at a time, into a wooden dish, and with a rolling-pin or beetle break and mash every one; transferring them, as they are done, into a large stone jar
2. Pour the boiling water upon the mashed gooseberries; cover the jar, and let them stand twelve hours
3. Then strain and measure the juice, and to each quart allow three-quarters of a pound of loaf-sugar
4. Mix it with the liquid, and let it stand eight or nine hours to dissolve, stirring it several times
5. Then pour it into a keg of proper size for containing it, and let it ferment at the bung-hole; filling it up as it works out with some of the liquor reserved for that purpose
6. As soon as it ceases to hiss, stop it close with a cloth wrapped round the bung
7. A pint of white brandy for every gallon of the gooseberry wine may be added on bunging it up
8. At the end of four or five months it will probably be fine enough to bottle off
9. You may refine it by allowing to every gallon of wine the whites of two eggs, beaten to a froth, with a very small tea-spoonful of salt
10. When the white of egg, &c. is a stiff froth, take out a quart of the wine, and mix them well together
11. Then pour it into the cask, and in a few days it will be fine and clear
12. Put two or three raisins in the bottom of each bottle
13. Keep the bottles in saw-dust, lying on their sides
